newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Quiet funeral for Bokassa starts in Bangui.
newsitem.headline: Quiet funeral for Bokassa starts in Bangui.

text.p: Family members on Monday attended the start of a low-key funeral for former Central African emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa, whose burial has been delayed by a crippling army mutiny in the capital Bangui.
Bokassa's body was moved from the Bangui General Hospital morgue to the city centre villa where he spent his last days before he died of a heart attack on November 3, aged 75.
The late emperor, whose eccentric life swung from surreal extravagance to exile and imprisonment, then lay in state in his full field marshal's uniform.

Family members and friends milled around the body in a giant glass-topped mahogany coffin built by a local craftsman. There was no sign of state protocol except for the discreet presence of Health Minister Cecile Fara-Front who represented the government at the lifting of the body from the hospital.
A notable absence was former empress Catherine who was nowhere to be seen among the family.
Bokassa seized power in 1966. He crowned himself emperor of the diamond-rich but impoverished nation in a lavish ceremony in 1977, only to be ousted in a French-backed coup in 1979.

A mass, also restricted to family and friends, will take place at the capital's Roman Catholic cathedral on Tuesday before the body leaves in a cortege for a private burial in his ancestral village of Berengo, 80 km (50 miles) south of Bangui.

Plans for a state funeral were blocked by an army revolt which erupted on November 16. A scheduled burial on December 10 was postponed by family and organisers citing security worries amid fighting between mutineers and loyalists troops.
The planned route will traverse rebel strongholds of the capital, where mutineers have clashed with troops loyal to President Ange-Felix Patasse.
Mutineers are mainly from the Yakoma tribe, while Bokassa's Ngbaka people are well represented in the army.

During a more violent army uprising last May, Bokassa came out publicly in support of rebel soldiers, whose grievances over pay and conditions have now turned into political demands including Patasse's resignation.
Many rebel soldiers believe the government should show more recognition, for the ex-dictator, whose humiliation included a trial for murder and imprisonment.
